title: Opioid Users Found a ‘Miracle Drug’ to Help Them Quit. Then the DEA Banned It
gist: In late August the DEA emergency-scheduled SR-17018, a compound developed with NIDA funding at USF, as a Schedule I substance. In mice it relieved pain without respiratory depression, and users online credit it with helping them taper off opioids without withdrawal. Researcher Laura Bohn says the ban halts her plans for human trials, and lawyer Robert Rush warns it could help set up another overdose crisis.

insights.claim: NIDA-funded research published in Cell in 2017 found that SR-17018 could relieve pain in mice without causing respiratory depression, which is typically what kills people who overdose on opioids.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A non-respiratory-depressing opioid analgesic would be a major advance in pain and addiction treatment.
insights.locator: Funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse

insights.claim: Mice using SR-17018 did not build high tolerance, and mice already dependent on morphine could use it to reset their tolerance without painful withdrawal.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A tolerance-resetting compound could compete with long-term maintenance therapies in opioid dependence treatment.

insights.claim: Laura Bohn's team at University of South Florida Health filed a patent on SR-17018, and the compound has never been tested in clinical trials in humans.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: The asset is patented but clinically unproven, so any commercial value depends on trials that are now blocked.

themes.theme: DEA emergency scheduling and its research impact

insights.claim: In late August the DEA emergency-scheduled SR-17018 as a Schedule I substance, alongside three other synthetic opioids, putting it in the same category as heroin.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Schedule I status sharply raises the cost and difficulty of developing the compound into a drug.
insights.quote: no currently accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse
insights.locator: But all of that came crashing

insights.claim: Bohn says the scheduling blocks her planned additional safety studies because she can no longer have the compound made, shipped or handled.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Regulatory scheduling can freeze an early-stage drug pipeline outright.
insights.quote: I can't have it made, I can't ship it, I can't touch it. I can't do anything.
insights.locator: For Bohn, the move will make

insights.claim: The DEA justified the scheduling with two forensic samples of SR-17018 found in two states since 2025 via NFLIS, plus some detections on the West Coast by the RaDAR monitoring system.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Shows how little detection evidence the DEA needs to trigger emergency scheduling, a regulatory risk for novel compounds.
insights.locator: In response to a request for comment

insights.claim: The emergency scheduling lasts two years with a possible one-year extension, during which no judge can review the decision, though permanent scheduling would require public and scientific input.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Sets a two-to-three-year window before SR-17018's regulatory status can be challenged or resolved.
insights.locator: The emergency scheduling will last two years

insights.claim: Attorney Robert Rush, who represents Bohn, says he petitioned the DEA to stop the scheduling on the grounds of SR-17018's lower risk profile, got no response, and calls the use of emergency powers draconian since the drug hasn't been linked to ER visits or overdose deaths.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Possible legal and policy challenges to DEA emergency scheduling practice.

insights.claim: Users on Reddit and Discord call SR-17018 a godsend for quitting opioids; one user says he tapered off MGM-15 in about three weeks with no physical withdrawal and no euphoria.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Anecdotal real-world demand suggests a gap in current addiction treatment, but there is no clinical evidence yet.
insights.quote: They've never created anything like this

insights.claim: Both users interviewed prefer SR-17018 to buprenorphine and methadone because it doesn't need to be taken long-term, while coming off those maintenance drugs can cause intense withdrawal.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A short-course tapering drug could threaten the long-duration revenue model of opioid maintenance therapies.
insights.locator: Both men have used gold-standard drugs

insights.claim: One user speculates the federal government banned SR-17018 because it saw it as a potential disruptor to a multibillion-dollar maintenance-drug industry.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Frames opioid maintenance treatment as an incumbent industry that a short-course compound could disrupt.
insights.quote: potential disruptor to a multibillion-dollar industry

insights.claim: The DEA has also placed 7-OH, a concentrated kratom compound sold through outlets like vape shops, and the related MGM-15 into Schedule I this summer.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: The gas-station opioid market is being shut down by federal scheduling, affecting retailers and suppliers.
insights.locator: He eventually graduated to a similar chemical

themes.theme: Policy risk of a new overdose wave

insights.claim: Robert Rush warns that banning gas station opioids like 7-OH while also removing potentially helpful substances like SR-17018 is setting up a perfect storm for another overdose crisis.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Removing supply without treatment options could worsen overdose trends, with public health and policy consequences.
insights.quote: is setting up a perfect storm for another overdose crisis
insights.locator: He says that the DEA banning

insights.claim: The DEA argues that because SR-17018 can reset opioid tolerance it may leave users more vulnerable to overdose, though the article notes the same is true of abstinence.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: The DEA's safety rationale is contestable, which could matter in a permanent scheduling fight.
